data.title: Hrádok nad Váhom – a Great Moravian hillfort and a hoard of 247 currency bars
data.excerpt: The hillfort at Hrádok was first described, surveyed and drawn by the Slovak scholar Štefan Janšák in 1930: a tongue-shaped promontory 200 m long, rising 10 m above its surroundings and occupied as early as the Iron Age. Its greatest fame came in 1955 with a hoard of 247 iron axe-shaped currency bars, for a long time the largest hoard of its kind in the whole of Czechoslovakia.

children.text: The hillfort was first described, surveyed and drawn by the brilliant Slovak scholar Štefan Janšák in 1930. The north-western part of the village of Hrádok, in which the church also stands, was occupied as early as the Iron Age.

For us it is important that in this part of the village our Slavic ancestors built an important hillfort in the times of Great Moravia. In his description of the hillfort Štefan Janšák states that the tongue-shaped promontory, 200 m long, on average 40 m wide and rising 10 m above its surroundings, was a very advantageous place for early occupation. The hillfort (see the picture below) extended over roughly the area a-b-e-c-d-f-a. The sector a-b-e-f-a may have been the core, separated from the rest of the surface by a natural step at e-f. Of the hollow c-d, which lies by the church and through which a street of the village now runs, it cannot be said today with certainty whether it is artificial or natural. In any case, however, it served the hillfort only to its benefit.

The historic stone castle of a later period stood in the sector a-b-e-f-a, where in the 1930s there was a farmstead with a garden and a cultivated field. At present the area of the hillfort holds gardens, houses and the church mentioned. Štefan Janšák found several sherds on the hillfort, which he assigned to the Hallstatt period.

children.text: The hoard of axe-shaped currency bars on the hillfort

When a refuse pit was being dug in the parsonage garden in 1954, an occupation layer was struck, from which an iron buckle, part of a horse bit and Slavic sherds dated to the 9th century come. The hillfort, however, became most famous for the find of a great hoard of axe-shaped currency bars in 1955, which for a long time was the largest hoard of such bars in the whole of Czechoslovakia.

children.text: The hoard was struck while the foundations for a new fence of the precinct of the Local National Committee were being dug in a road cutting, at a depth of c. 100 cm. The find spot lies directly within the precinct of the Great Moravian hillfort. The pit in which the hoard had been deposited reached 40 cm into the loess subsoil. The upper part of the hoard was covered by a medieval made-up layer of the 13th – 14th centuries. The hoard contained 247 iron axe-shaped currency bars, mostly of medium size (114 pieces 250–300 mm long) and 68 smaller pieces 165–1200 mm long. The rest consisted of fragments of bars. On some of the bars an intentional cutting off of part of the piece can be observed, or trapezoidal or triangular notches. Some also bear signs of reforging. After it was found the hoard weighed c. 65 kg, and the bars in it were stacked in little piles of 20 pieces. The find is dated to the 9th century and its deposition may be connected with the troubled times of the conflict between Prince Pribina and Mojmír, as was also the case with nearby Pobedim. An inhabitant of the hillfort – perhaps a merchant who used the bars as currency, or another, undoubtedly wealthy inhabitant of the Váh region – deposited the hoard out of fear that he would lose his property. Since no one ever came back for this hoard, which must have had a very high value in the times of the Principality of Nitra, its owner evidently lost something more precious than the bars – his own life.
